name: Fit-focused dressing for body type (shoulder-to-waist illusion)

card.summary: Cuts and fit chosen to show off a V-taper; popular in style advice, untested as a clothing intervention.
card.aka: V-taper dressing, tailoring for body type

quick.overview:
This is the practice of choosing clothing cut and fit to emphasise a broad-shoulder, narrow-waist look and downplay other areas.

Body-shape literature links wide shoulders and a narrow waist to perceived attractiveness, but no study has tested whether specific clothing cuts produce that effect.
quick.mechanism: Fit and tailoring change where garments sit and how much volume they add, which practitioners say alters the apparent shoulder-to-waist proportion.
quick.risks: No health risks are documented for ordinary clothing choices.

lead: Fit-focused dressing means choosing and tailoring clothes to emphasise a V-shaped torso, with broad shoulders tapering to a narrower waist, and to minimise features a wearer sees as flaws. Clothing that follows the shoulder line and takes in fabric at the waist makes the shoulder-to-waist contrast look larger, which is how people use it to look more athletic and proportioned without changing their body.[1][2]

The V shape, called the inverted triangle, is one of the described male body shapes: wider shoulders and chest, a narrow waist and a broad upper body.[1] Wikipedia notes that men commonly have wider shoulders and latissimus dorsi that give the torso this shape, and that waist-to-chest ratio in men has been studied for appeal to women.[1]

Research on attractiveness has examined body proportions rather than clothing. In 2023, Pazhoohi, Garza and Kingstone reported across four studies with 659 heterosexual women that men with larger shoulder-to-hip ratios, and taller men, were rated as more attractive, masculine and capable fighters.[3] No published trial was found testing whether particular garment cuts change how attractive a man is rated.

chain: Tailored cuts follow the shoulder line and take in the waist
Greater visual contrast between shoulders and waist
angle.text: Fit changes how the existing frame reads: clothing that fits the shoulders and trims excess fabric around the waist makes the V-taper more visible. Lifters in forums describe this as the main reason they use tailors and athletic-cut shirts.

infobox: Emphasise a V-taper; de-emphasise perceived frame flaws

paras: Body shape is shaped by skeletal structure and by muscle and fat distribution; skeletal structure stops growing in the teen years while muscle and fat can change.[1] Men's shapes are commonly described as inverted triangle, rectangle or apple.[1] The article describes android fat distribution in men, in which fat sits in the trunk and upper body, and says testosterone supports muscle growth, with shoulder widening and ribcage expansion occurring in puberty.[1]

Practitioners describe tailoring and fit choices intended to make shoulders look broader relative to the waist. Garment sizing in general is based on chest, waist and hip measurements, and posture affects those measurements.[1]

Wikipedia's article on tailors says a bespoke suit involves a skeleton fitting in which the partly made garment is adjusted, and that nearly 75 percent of the stitching of a custom-tailored suit is still done by hand.[4] It defines a tailor as someone who makes or alters clothing, especially men's clothing.[4]

On T Nation, posters with muscular builds describe the problem fit-focused dressing addresses. One writes that even athletic or tailored-fit dress shirts have too much fabric around the waist and that off-the-rack suits cut to fit the chest and shoulders are too boxy, so they had their suits tailored to fit.[5] Another says they want an athletic cut, meaning v-tapered, and finds suits problematic.[6] A third says they cannot find a tailor willing to remove enough material for a drastic v-taper.[7]

Pazhoohi and colleagues' 2023 Archives of Sexual Behavior paper tested height and shoulder-to-hip ratio together and found a height by ratio interaction only when both varied and stimuli were realistic enough, such as silhouettes versus rendered figures.[3] A 2023 EEG study by Pazhoohi, Arantes, Kingstone and Pinal found that participants rated larger shoulder-to-hip ratios as more attractive regardless of the sex of stimulus or participant.[3]

A 2021 study by Garza and Byrd-Craven in 130 women found that those with a stronger short-term mating orientation were more attracted to men with low waist-to-chest ratios, and that women who saw themselves as attractive rated low-ratio men higher.[3] Wikipedia also cites Singh (2007), who argued that body shape reflects hormone levels during puberty.[1]
No studies found testing clothing fit or tailoring as an intervention. Related research on body proportions and perceived attractiveness exists, but it concerns bodies rather than clothing.[3]

lore.intro: In T Nation threads, lifters discuss how their trained shoulders and narrow waists fit poorly in off-the-rack shirts and suits, and trade views on tailoring.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: Tailoring is needed to show a V-taper in dress clothes
claims.believers: Posters say off-the-rack shirts and suits have too much fabric at the waist for trained builds and that tailored suits present properly.[5]
claims.experts: No published study has tested tailoring or garment cuts for effects on perceived attractiveness; studies concern body proportions such as shoulder-to-hip ratio.[3]

claims.claim: A broad-shouldered, narrow-waisted silhouette is more attractive
claims.believers: Lifters train for the V-taper and dress to show it.[7]
claims.experts: A 2023 series of studies with 659 women found larger shoulder-to-hip ratios were rated as more attractive, masculine and capable fighters.[3]
